paragraphs.text: Desktop notifications for DeepSeek Harness (dsh) Web sessions: get notified when a session waits for
approval or finishes, then click to jump back to it.
# System Notifications · DeepSeek Harness plugin

A **client-only** plugin for the DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`) Web UI that raises a desktop
notification
when a session needs you, and jumps back to that session when you click it.

- A session **waits for permission approval / an answer / a plan review** → notification.
- A sessio

n **finishes a run** (`running` flips `true → false`) → notification.
- **Clicking** the notificatio

n brings the browser window to the front and opens that session.
- Settings live in **Settings → Gen
eral → System Notifications**.

Notifications are edge-triggered: the first snapshot after page load is taken as the baseline,
so a
refresh never floods you with a backlog.

> Version 1.2.0 — a second General row, **Persistent notifications**, asks the OS to keep a
> notifi

cation on screen until you click or dismiss it (Web Notification `requireInteraction`).
>
> Version

1.1.0 — notification titles name the **project** (`Project · Event`,
> e.g. `harness-plugins · Appro
val required`), and the body names the session.
## Requirements

- DeepSeek Harness with plugin support (`engines.dsh: >=0.2.1-rc.2`), Web GUI served in a
Chromium-b

ased browser (Chrome/Edge). `http://127.0.0.1` is a secure context, so no HTTPS is
required for the

Notification API.
- The page must stay open — notifications are raised by the page's JavaScript, not

API.
- The page must stay open — notifications are raised by the page's JavaScript, not by the host.
## Install
The package is not published on npm yet; install it straight from this repository:
[代码示例省略，未执行]

Or in the Web UI: **Plugins → Install**, and paste
`github:purejiang/dsh-system-notifications`.

The plugin is build-free: it ships `index.js` (an empty host half that registers the bundle row)
and
`client.js` (the whole feature). Refreshing the page after install is enough.
## Enable and test

1. Open **Settings → General → System Notifications** and switch it on.
2. Grant the browser's notif

ication permission. The plugin asks once, on your **first click or
keypress** after the page loads;

you can also use the **Authorize** button in the same row.
If you dismissed or denied the prompt, al

low `http://127.0.0.1:3080` in
`chrome://settings/content/notifications` (or the site icon in the ad

dress bar) and retry.
3. Optional: turn on the second row, **Persistent notifications**, to keep eac

h notification on
screen until you click or dismiss it. It is off by default; Windows may still rout

e the toast
to the notification center instead of leaving it on top.
4. The **Test notification** bu

tton is hidden in the shipped UI. To use it, double-click the
row title “System Notifications” (stor

ed per session in `sessionStorage`), or open the page
with `?dshNotificationTest=1`.
## Behaviour

- **When:** a new `pendingInteraction` appears (`approval`, `question`, or `plan-review`), or
`runni

ng` changes from `true` to `false`.
- **Title:** `<project> · <event>`. The project is the title of

the workspace that owns the
session (the default workspace is localized, e.g. “Default Workspace”);

if the workspace list
is not loaded yet it falls back to the directory name of the session's `cwd`.

- **Body:** the session's display title plus the reason, e.g.
““Refactor the toolbar” requests to ru

n bash and is waiting for your approval.”
Approval notifications include the tool name; completion n

otifications include the elapsed
time when the plugin observed the whole run.
- **Icon:** the embedd

ed 128×128 DeepSeek whale mark (PNG data URL, no external requests).
- **Quiet while you watch:** no

notification while that session's conversation panel is visible
and the window has focus.
- **No no

ise:** subagent sessions are skipped, duplicate notifications collapse per session
(`tag`), and at m

ost 6 notifications are kept open.
- **Persistent mode (optional):** when enabled, notifications set

`requireInteraction` so the OS
keeps the toast up until the user acts on it, instead of hiding it a
fter the default timeout.
## Settings rows

Both rows are built from the host's own primitives (`Switch`/`Button` from
`@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-

ui-primitives`), so their spacing and type match the built-in settings
rows. The main row shows the

current state and explains why notifications are off when the
browser permission is denied; the seco
nd row controls persistent notifications.
## How it works
Everything is done through documented client extension points; no host-side code is needed:
| Need | Extension point |

| Detect waiting / finished | `shell.overlay` component reading `props.useSessionStatus()` |
| Sessi

on title | `props.useSessions()` → `SessionListState.byId[id].displayTitle` |
| Project name | `prop

s.useWorkspaces()` (workspace title / session ownership), fallback to `cwd` |
| Am I looking at it |

`props.usePanelInfo().activePanelId`, `document.hasFocus()`, `visibilityState` |
| Raise the notifi

cation | the browser `Notification` API |
| Click → open session | `ctx.get('uiWorkspace').openSessi

on(sessionId)` |
| Settings controls | `settings.general.item` |

The `running` transition is observed both through React snapshots and by subscribing to the
client `

uiSession.sessionStatus` store, because background tabs throttle rendering and would
otherwise coale
sce a short run into no visible change.

## Limitations

- The page must remain open; a closed tab cannot notify.
- Notification layout (font, colour, extra

buttons) is controlled by the browser and the OS.
- Clicking an old notification after a page reload

focuses the window but may not reopen the
session (the page context is gone).
- Notification titles

are truncated by the OS; the project name is placed first so it stays
visible.
- If the browser per

mission is denied, nothing is sent and the settings row states the reason.
- Persistent mode is best

-effort: some platforms ignore `requireInteraction` and fall back to
the normal notification timeout

effort: some platforms ignore `requireInteraction` and fall back to
the normal notification timeout.
